steps.label: KP08 Two extremes and the compromise
Two extremes · 1/6
steps.speakerNotes: Single-sample SGD is cheap but each step has high variance and the path jitters like a drunkard, leaving most of the GPU idle; the full batch has no noise but scans all data per step and often exceeds memory.

steps.label: Two extremes · 1/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Single sample: lowest cost, largest noise, poor hardware use.

steps.label: Two extremes · 1/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A minibatch sits in the middle: medium cost and noise, with a batch's forward and backward packed into matrix multiplications that run in parallel on a GPU.

steps.label: Two extremes · 1/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Full batch: highest cost, zero noise, often too big for memory.

steps.label: Two extremes · 1/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: A minibatch updates with the average gradient of the batch.

steps.label: Two extremes · 1/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: It remains unbiased and averaging lowers the variance.

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6
steps.speakerNotes: The standard way: shuffle the whole training set, then cut it into disjoint batches. With n 1000 and batch 32 we get 31 full batches using 992 samples.

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: 8 samples are left.

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Using every batch once is one epoch: 31 updates, each sample seen exactly once.

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The 8 leftovers can serve as a smaller batch or be dropped; the next epoch reshuffles so a different set is dropped.

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: the 8 leftovers use as a smaller batch or drop them (drop_last): the next epoch reshuffles

steps.label: Batches and epochs · 2/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: The other is sampling with replacement, where batches may overlap; drawing n times covers about 63.2 percent unique samples. Deep learning prefers without replacement.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6
steps.speakerNotes: With the four samples at w equal 5 the single gradients are 3, 1, minus 1, minus 3 with mean 0.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The batch of samples one and two averages 2.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The batch of samples three and four averages minus 2.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The full average is 0.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: A minibatch estimate can point opposite to the full gradient, yet the two batches average exactly 0.

steps.label: A batch estimate · 3/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: The six possible two-sample batch averages are 2, 1, 0, 0, minus 1, minus 2 with standard deviation 1.291; a single sample has 2.236; the full batch 0. Variance falls with batch size.

steps.label: Variance formulas · 4/6
steps.speakerNotes: For independent sampling with replacement, the batch average's variance is sigma squared over b.

steps.label: Variance formulas · 4/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Without replacement multiply by the finite-population correction, n minus b over n minus 1.

steps.label: Variance formulas · 4/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Check: n equal 4, b equal 2: 5 over 2 times 2 over 3 equals 5 over 3, standard deviation 1.291.

steps.label: Variance formulas · 4/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: It equals the 1.291 computed directly from the six batches.

steps.label: Variance formulas · 4/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: equal to the 1.291 computed directly from the six batches “variance is always \sigma^2/b” holds only for independent draws

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6
steps.speakerNotes: Batch size controls three things. First, noise: smaller as the batch grows.

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, memory: heavier as the batch grows.

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Third, updates per epoch: fewer as the batch grows.

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: updates per epoch \lfloor n/b\rfloor, fewer as b grows

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: An epoch is not a universal unit of compute: ten epochs with batch 10 is a thousand updates, with batch 100 only a hundred.

steps.label: Trade-offs · 5/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: So compare two training setups by update count and samples seen, not by epochs alone.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “a larger batch is always better”. more precise steps, but fewer updates and tighter memory

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “a minibatch estimate is always near the full gradient”. a single batch can point the opposite way

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “same epochs means same amount of training”. update count and samples seen are the amounts

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: With noise present, what does “convergence” even mean?
